opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think memory is going to be really important, and it's kind of two things. One is just within a single task. As these research tasks get longer and more complex, the agent is reading a huge number of sources, trying different search strategies, hitting dead ends, and backtracking. At some point you run up against the limits of the context window, so the model needs a way to keep track of what it's already found, what it's already tried, and what the open questions still are, without having to hold every token of every web page in context at once. Getting good at deciding what to keep and what to summarize or drop is a real capability we need to build.

The other piece is memory across tasks. Right now, every time you ask for a deep research report, it's starting more or less from scratch. But if you're a person who uses it a lot, maybe you're an analyst covering a particular industry, or you're researching a medical condition for a family member, there's a lot of context about you that would make the output so much better: what you already know, what sources you trust, what format you like, what you asked about last week. Having to re-explain all of that every time is a lot of friction. A really good human research assistant gets better the longer they work with you, because they learn your preferences and build up background knowledge. I think we want the agent to feel that way too.

So as tasks go from taking a few minutes to potentially hours or days, and as people start relying on these agents for ongoing work rather than one-off questions, memory goes from a nice-to-have to something that's really core to making the agent useful.

r001.rationale: It says memory can retain user-specific context such as what they know, trusted sources, preferred formats, and prior questions, avoiding the friction of re-explaining these for each task.

r002.rationale: It describes learning user preferences and building background knowledge across tasks, but does not clearly say that new research builds on prior research findings.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think memory becomes really important as the tasks get longer and more complex, for a few reasons.

The first is just the practical one. When you're doing a deep research task, the model might be browsing hundreds of pages, running searches, going down different paths, and a lot of that doesn't need to stay in context. So you need some way of managing what the model is holding onto at any given time, and deciding what's actually relevant to the final answer versus what was a dead end. Right now a lot of that is handled by context management, but as tasks get longer, I think you need something more like real memory, where the model can store intermediate findings and come back to them later.

The second thing is that a lot of the most valuable research tasks aren't one-shot. If I'm doing a project over a week, I don't want to start from scratch every time. I want the agent to remember what we looked at yesterday, what sources I trusted and didn't trust, what I already decided wasn't worth pursuing. That's a lot of what makes a good research assistant good. They build up context about the problem and about you over time.

And then there's the personalization side. The same question means different things depending on who's asking. If you know someone's background, what level of detail they want, what they already know, you can give a much better answer. Memory is how you get there.

So I think of it as, the model is already pretty good at doing a single hard task. Memory is what lets it compound over multiple tasks, and that's where the really interesting stuff starts to happen.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent should remember a user’s background, preferences, trusted sources, and prior decisions over time so the user does not have to start from scratch on each task.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says memory lets research compound across multiple tasks and describes returning to prior findings and decisions.

astra-6.text:
I think as you give these agents longer, more complex tasks, you want them to build on what they’ve already learned. If an agent spends a lot of time researching something with you, you don’t want the next task to start from scratch. You want it to remember the context, what you care about, and the feedback you gave it.

And within a research task, there’s a lot to keep track of: which directions it’s explored, what evidence it’s found, what questions are still open. Memory helps make that work cumulative. The hard part is deciding what to retain and when to bring it back, because remembering everything isn’t necessarily useful. You want the relevant context, and you want the agent to be able to update it as it learns more.

r001.rationale: It says the next task should not start from scratch and the agent should remember the user’s context, preferences, and feedback, which avoids repeating that information.

r002.rationale: It says agents should build on what they have already learned and that research work should be cumulative across tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think as you give an agent more complex tasks, it becomes increasingly important that it can build on work it’s already done. With deep research, you might spend a lot of time exploring a question, finding sources, and figuring out which avenues are useful. You don’t want the agent to have to rediscover all of that every time you ask a follow-up.

And there’s also context about you: what you’re trying to accomplish, what you already know, what you consider a good answer. Memory can help the agent carry that context forward, so you can delegate more without having to write an incredibly detailed prompt every time.

The challenge is deciding what to remember and when to use it. You want it to retain useful findings, but also be able to revisit them when new information comes in.

r001.rationale: It says memory can carry forward what the user is trying to accomplish, already knows, and considers a good answer, reducing the need for a detailed prompt each time.

r002.rationale: It argues that agents should build on prior work and avoid rediscovering research findings when handling follow-ups.
